item.title: Navatu coach challenges North: Prepare to win
item.description: NAVATU Secondary School under-19 head coach Alipate Ravulo has thrown down the challenge to schools and teams in the North — prepare to win, not simply to participate. item.content:encoded:
NAVATU Secondary School under-19 head coach Alipate Ravulo has thrown down the challenge to schools and teams in the North — prepare to win, not simply to participate.

Ravulo’s message comes after his side created history as the first northern school team to ever reach the Vodafone Super Deans Championship U19 final, becoming the lone northern school to carry the division’s hopes on the biggest stage of Fiji’s secondary school rugby competition.

For Ravulo, the achievement is proof that northern schools have the ability to compete with their Viti Levu counterparts when given the right preparation.

His challenge to other northern teams is simple but profound: preparation must be purposeful.

“Prepare to win, don’t prepare to participate,” Ravulo said.

He believes preparation must go beyond physical conditioning and rugby skills, with teams needing to cater for the physical, mental and spiritual aspects of their players.

Ravulo said northern teams should not see themselves as inferior to schools from Viti Levu.

“We are all the same. Whether we are from Viti Levu or Vanua Levu, we are all human. We just need to prepare well,” he said.

More importantly, Ravulo believes northern schools should have no excuses after Navatu’s historic run.

The school does not have its own rugby ground or gym and has had to work with very limited resources, yet its U19 side has fought its way into the national final.

If Navatu can reach the biggest stage despite those limitations, Ravulo believes schools in the North with better facilities and greater resources should be capable of achieving even more.

“Navatu’s achievement should tell every school in the North that it is possible,” is the message behind Ravulo’s challenge.

His words carry added weight because Navatu’s campaign has demonstrated what can be achieved when belief, discipline and preparation are placed ahead of circumstances.

The message was echoed by his captain and standout player, Vilimone Kanawabu, who has emerged as one of the competition’s leading performers.

Despite attending school in the North, Kanawabu broke into the Fiji Schoolboys team last year, showing that talent from Vanua Levu can earn recognition at national level.

Kanawabu believes the formula for achieving rugby goals is equally straightforward.

He said unwavering faith, coupled with hard work, was the secret behind reaching one’s goals.

item.title: Breaking barriers, making history
item.description: JASMINE Daunakamakama says winning a historic Commonwealth Games boxing medal was an overwhelming experience after years of dedication, sacrifice and resilience. Daunakamakama became the first Fijian woman to win a Commonwealth Games medal in boxing after securing bronze at the Games.
item.content:encoded:
JASMINE Daunakamakama says winning a historic Commonwealth Games boxing medal was an overwhelming experience after years of dedication, sacrifice and resilience.

Daunakamakama became the first Fijian woman to win a Commonwealth Games medal in boxing after securing bronze at the Games.

For the 23-year-old boxer, the achievement was the fulfilment of a dream she had carried since childhood.

Daunakamakama said she had started writing down her goals when she was 10 years old, long before she knew where her boxing journey would take her.

“I remember writing my goals down from 10 years old,” she said.

She said the moment she first picked up a pair of boxing gloves created a spark that continued to grow as she committed herself to the sport.

“It felt unreal but real at the same time because I had done the work,” Daunakamakama said.

She said she had dedicated herself to boxing physically, mentally and spiritually, making the Commonwealth Games medal even more meaningful.

“It was an overwhelming experience,” she said.

However, Daunakamakama said it was not until she returned to Fiji and visited her village that she was able to fully appreciate the significance of the achievement.

She shared her medal with members of her community and said seeing them celebrate and treasure it as their own helped ground the experience.

“It allowed me to appreciate the achievement just as much,” she said.

The medal also represented a significant moment in a career that has included both highs and lows.

Daunakamakama, who is in her third year in the elite division, said her journey had tested her physically and mentally and required her to remain focused despite setbacks.

She credited her parents, support system, coach and the Fiji boxing team for helping her stay on the right pathway.

“They have really been a rock in this experience for me,” she said.

“They have been just as disciplined as I am and I’m just a reflection of the people around me.”

Daunakamakama said boxing came with several challenges, including managing her weight while maintaining the level of performance required at international competitions.

She also reflected on the disappointment surrounding her experience at last year’s Liverpool World Championships, where a missed gender test affected her participation.

Rather than allowing the setback to define her, Daunakamakama said she used it as a lesson in resilience.

“I kept my head up and I think I learned the lesson of being resilient,” she said.

“No matter what the outcome is, I will stay true to myself and continue to practise integrity through the process.”

Daunakamakama believes remaining committed to the process will eventually produce results.

Her Commonwealth Games achievement has also placed her in a position to inspire the next generation of female athletes.

She urged young girls and women to take the time to understand themselves, block out negative voices and refuse to be limited by stereotypes or fear.

“Block out the noise, block out the stereotypes that are pushed on you,” she said.

“you are more than capable of greatness once you strip all of that away.”

Daunakamakama said young people should pursue whatever they are passionate about, whether it is sport, music, dance or another field.

item.description: A WINNING culture built on accountability and a strong return on investment will be the key performance measure as the Fiji Rugby Union begins its search for a new FIJI Water Flying Fijians head coach. item.content:encoded:
A WINNING culture built on accountability and a strong return on investment will be the key performance measure as the Fiji Rugby Union begins its search for a new FIJI Water Flying Fijians head coach.

Fiji Rugby Union board chairman John Sanday said the Flying Fijians were the organisation’s flagship business asset and the new coach would be expected to deliver wins and consistency while helping elevate the Fiji Rugby brand globally.

“The Board has set clear goals and expectations of the performance standards required,” Sunday said.

“The Flying Fijians is Fiji Rugby’s flagship business asset and we are expecting wins and consistency to support brand elevation globally.

“A strong work ethic centred around accountability plus return on investment are the key performance metrics we will be pushing. We want a winning culture, simple as that.”

The head coach position has been advertised as part of a global search being conducted by an overseas professional recruitment firm.

The firm will evaluate the applications before candidates are considered by the selection panel.

Sunday said the process was open to all eligible applicants, including interim Flying Fijians coach Senirusi Seruvakula and newly appointed Fijian Drua head coach Brad Mooar.

“Senirusi is free to submit an application,” Sunday said.

“The same applies to Brad Mooar, anyone can apply.”

Seruvakula was appointed on a temporary basis before the Flying Fijians’ Nations Cup matches in July, with the FRU now proceeding with the recruitment process as it looks towards the 2027 Rugby World Cup and beyond.

Sunday said past performance would not necessarily determine the outcome, with all applications to be assessed on their strengths and how they fit Fiji Rugby’s expectations.

The successful candidate will therefore be expected to deliver more than results, with accountability, consistency, a strong work ethic and return on investment forming the foundation of the board’s expectations.

With the 2027 Rugby World Cup approaching, the FRU wants the Flying Fijians to establish a sustained winning culture and strengthen Fiji Rugby’s global brand.

item.title: New faces bolster Fiji’s title defence
item.description: THE FIJI Water Flying Fijians will enter their Asahi Pacific Nations Cup title defence with six potential debutants, while the return of Tuidraki Samusamuvodre gives the side another attacking option as Fiji builds towards the 2027 Rugby World Cup. Among the new faces are Penaia Cakobau, Vilikesa Nairau, Inoke Ravuiwasa, Isoa Tuwai, Terio Tamani and Isaac Ratumaitavuki-Kneepkens.
item.content:encoded:
THE FIJI Water Flying Fijians will enter their Asahi Pacific Nations Cup title defence with six potential debutants, while the return of Tuidraki Samusamuvodre gives the side another attacking option as Fiji builds towards the 2027 Rugby World Cup.

Among the new faces are Penaia Cakobau, Vilikesa Nairau, Inoke Ravuiwasa, Isoa Tuwai, Terio Tamani and Isaac Ratumaitavuki-Kneepkens.

Their selection provides acting head coach Senirusi Seruvakula with an opportunity to expand Fiji’s Test depth while introducing players who have impressed through the domestic and professional pathway.

Tuwai’s inclusion is particularly significant.

The flanker was named in the Flying Fijians squad for last year’s Pacific Nations Cup and was one of three uncapped players selected at the time. However, he did not take the field and remains uncapped. His return gives him another opportunity to finally make his Test debut.

Samusamuvodre, meanwhile, returns to the squad looking to add to the two Test caps he earned during last year’s tournament.

The outside back made his Flying Fijians debut against Samoa in 2025 and was part of a group of players who were given their first opportunity at international level.

His pace and ability to operate across the outside backs could provide Fiji with another attacking weapon, particularly as the team continues to develop its options ahead of the World Cup.

Tamani also offers a different dimension after establishing himself in rugby sevens, while Ratumaitavuki-Kneepkens brings versatility to the backline.

Cakobau, Nairau and Ravuiwasa will provide further competition among the forwards, with their inclusion allowing the coaching staff to assess the next layer of players capable of stepping into Test rugby.

The squad will also have to cope without a number of France-based players.

Fiji’s leading Top 14-based internationals are unavailable because the Pacific Nations Cup falls outside the international Test window, meaning French clubs are not obliged to release their players for the tournament. The timing also coincides with the start of the Top 14 season and clubs’ pre-season preparations.

That has forced Fiji to look deeper into its player pool, but it could ultimately prove valuable as the Flying Fijians strengthen their depth before the 2027 Rugby World Cup.

Fiji’s record in the Pacific Nations Cup means expectations will remain high.

The Flying Fijians are the competition’s most successful team, having won the title seven times, including championships in 2013, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018 and back-to-back triumphs in 2024 and 2025.

Fiji retained the title last year after defeating Japan in the final, continuing its dominance of the competition.

The Flying Fijians begin their 2026 campaign against Canada in Japan on September 12.

item.title: World Surf League Championship Tour in Fiji
item.description: Fiji’s hosting of the 2026 Fiji Pro is more than a world-class surfing event. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Tourism and Civil Aviation Viliame Gavoka highlights its importance to tourism, sports, environmental protection and opportunities for Fijians.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji’s hosting of the 2026 Fiji Pro is more than a world-class surfing event.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Tourism and Civil Aviation Viliame Gavoka highlights its importance to tourism, sports, environmental protection and opportunities for Fijians.

Speaking at the official opening ceremony, Gavoka said Fiji was privileged to host Stop Number Eight of the 2026 World Surf League Championship Tour.

The 2026 Fiji Surfing Pro will feature 24 of the world’s best women and 36 men from 16 countries to Cloudbreak.

He described Cloudbreak as not only an extraordinary wave but a distinctly Fijian one, deeply connected to the country’s ocean, reefs, islands and communities.

“When millions of people around the world watch Cloudbreak, they are not only watching a surfing competition. They are seeing Fiji,” Gavoka said.

He stressed that the success of the event depended on the health of Fiji’s marine environment, saying there could be no Cloudbreak without a healthy reef and no sustainable tourism industry without healthy ecosystems.

Gavoka welcomed initiatives under the World Surf League’s One Ocean programme, which works with Conservation International, the Fiji Surfing Association and the Mamanuca Environment Society on environmental and community projects.

He said the Fiji Pro should also inspire young Fijians to pursue opportunities beyond competing, including coaching, hospitality, marine conservation, media, tourism and enterprise.

item.title: From 10 players to champions
item.description: RATU Nauvula College may have been the lone western school at the Vodafone Super Deans Championship finals, but its under-14 side ensured the West would not leave the HFC Bank National Stadium empty-handed last Saturday. The young Nauvula warriors produced one of the most inspiring stories of the finals, overcoming Queen Victoria School 22-17 to claim the U14 title and carry the hopes of the Weste
item.content:encoded:
RATU Nauvula College may have been the lone western school at the Vodafone Super Deans Championship finals, but its under-14 side ensured the West would not leave the HFC Bank National Stadium empty-handed last Saturday.

The young Nauvula warriors produced one of the most inspiring stories of the finals, overcoming Queen Victoria School 22-17 to claim the U14 title and carry the hopes of the Western Division with them.

For head coach Viliame Vuetaki, the triumph was the reward for a journey built on faith, hard work and perseverance.

“To be frankly honest, we started training in week one during round one of the competition and, like I said in the semi-finals, we only had two reserves,” Vuetaki said.

“It was only through the Lord that we were able to achieve this.”

The coach’s words reflected the remarkable determination within a team that had entered the competition with modest expectations.

Captain Vero Naovuka revealed that when the team first came together, there were only 10 players.

“When we started the team there were only 10 players. We didn’t expect to come this far, but we just prepared well, trained hard and listened to our coaches,” Naovuka said.

That belief was tested in the closing stages of the final.

With Nauvula holding a slender 22-17 lead inside the final five minutes, Naovuka said the message from the coaching bench was simple — remain calm and defend.

“I told the boys just keep defending and stay composed. When they lose the ball, it will be ours,” he recalled.

They defended their line, absorbed the pressure and refused to surrender the advantage that had taken months of sacrifice to build.

For Vuetaki, however, the victory belonged to more than just the team. He dedicated the achievement to Ratu Nauvula College, the vanua that had stood behind the team throughout its campaign and the parents who supported their children.

But the coach was quick to redirect the spotlight.

“The spotlight belongs to the players and the man above,” he said.

And fittingly, it was the players who wrote the final chapter.

From a team that started with just 10 players to a Deans championship-winning side, Nauvula’s U14 journey was a reminder that in schoolboy rugby, champions are not always built from numbers or reputation.

Sometimes they are built from belief, discipline, sacrifice and the courage to keep going.

On a day when the West stood alone among the finalists, Ratu Nauvula College stood tall.

The West had its champion — and it was a team that simply refused to give up.

Team manager Frances Qounadovu said the players gave their all throughout the co
item.content:encoded:
THE FMF Rewa Women’s Rugby team may have suffered another defeat 51-30 against Khelvin Civil Engineering Lautoka Women’s in the Subrails Marama Cup Championship, but their round four encounter provided a much-needed boost as the side finally found its way onto the scoreboard at Churchill Park in Lautoka last Saturday.

Team manager Frances Qounadovu said the players gave their all throughout the contest and welcomed the opportunity to compete again after three scoreless matches against Naitasiri, Malolo and Kadavu.

“It was a fair game, we loved every minute of it, the girls gave their all,” Qounadovu said.

After three consecutive games without points, getting on the scoreboard was an important achievement for a Rewa side that has endured a difficult opening to the competition.

The manager credited the players for their determination and thanked God for giving the team strength and the opportunity to experience the game again.

However, the manager acknowledged that there is still considerable work ahead, particularly in fitness, communication and technical skills.

The Rewa Women’s team has also faced challenges beyond the playing field, including limited technical assistance and the need for greater support for the players’ overall well-being.

Despite those difficulties, the team continues to represent young women from Serua, Ovalau and Rewa, bringing together players from different walks of life.

Frances thanked the various clubs within the Rewa Rugby Union, as well as the families who continue to support the players.

As the competition enters its fourth week, she appealed to the public to rally behind women’s rugby.

“One concern highlighted was the small crowd at the Marama Cup match, so I am urging supporters and the public to attend women matches and encourage their women’s team.

“Whatever the result, the Rewa Women’s Team is still there and are still fighting for this season,” Frances said.

The focus now turns to continued improvement and building on the positives from Round Four and more work on the fundamentals.

The Rewa Women’s team remains hopeful of better results as the Marama Cup Championship continues.

They will face Suva Women for Round 5 at the HFC Bank Stadium next weekend.

item.title: Nasoko franchise – A new beginning for schools rugby in Fiji
item.description: FOR generations, the final whistle of the Deans competition has signalled the end of the secondary schools rugby season. This week, however, that final whistle will signal something entirely different — the beginning of a new pathway.
item.content:encoded:
FOR generations, the final whistle of the Deans competition has signalled the end of the secondary schools rugby season.

This week, however, that final whistle will signal something entirely different — the beginning of a new pathway.

Fiji’s best young rugby players will come together under one banner when the inaugural Nasoko Franchise competition gets underway, bringing the cream of the Vodafone Super Deans and Raluve competitions into a unique national talent identification and development programme.

The initiative will unite the best under-16 and U18 boys and girls from the Eastern, Northern, Southern and Western zones for a week of rugby, assessment, education and development.

But the importance of Nasoko extends far beyond finding out which zone has the strongest team.

Fiji Rugby Union acting chief operations officer Talemo Waqa says that is not the purpose.

“The whole purpose there is for the cream of every zone to come and play together — east versus north, south versus west and so on,” Waqa said.

The teams will play a three-day round-robin competition from Tuesday to Thursday, giving coaches and selectors an opportunity to assess the country’s outstanding young talent.

Friday will then provide another dimension, with the players selected into new combinations for further matches.

“It is not there for whoever has won,” Waqa said.

“No, it’s there to put together formidable U16 and U18 teams, girls and boys.”

For the first time, Fiji Rugby is attempting to bring the best young talent from every corner of the country together immediately after the major secondary schools competitions.

The programme has been put together through the Ministry of Education, Fiji Rugby and the Fiji Secondary Schools Rugby Union, creating what could become the annual culmination of the schools rugby calendar.

“It has never been done in the past,” Waqa said.

“It is something that we believe is the way forward each year, so that we culminate in such a Nasoko competition.”

That vision could prove significant for the future of the sport.

For too long, the end of a schools competition has often meant the end of meaningful competition for many promising players.

Nasoko is designed to close that gap, allowing Fiji Rugby to immediately identify, assess and begin developing the country’s next generation.

It is also a programme built around more than players.

Coaches, managers, strength and conditioning personnel and match officials will all be part of the development environment, making Nasoko a complete rugby development exercise rather than simply another tournament.

The girls will be based at Namaka Public School, while the boys’ competition will be held in at Ba Provincial High School.
